## Overview

Clinical microbiome and microbial genome-wide association studies (mGWAS) link microbial community shifts, strain transmission, and bacterial genetic variation to patient phenotypes. This workflow adapts the clinical metagenomics archetypes from the VITALITY infant atopic dermatitis trial (Shen et al.) into standardized `cliomicplot` figure calls.

```r
library(cliomicplot)
library(ggplot2)
clitheme("nature")
```

```{r load-pkg, echo=FALSE}
library(cliomicplot)
library(ggplot2)
clitheme("nature")
```

---

## 1. Clinical Severity Stratification by Host Genetics

In cohort studies of atopic dermatitis, host genetic lesions (such as *FLG* loss-of-function variants) interact with microbial colonization. Here, clinical eczema severity (SCORAD index) is compared across disease subgroups with overlaid patient jitter and rank-sum tests:

```{r clinical-scorad, fig.width=6.0, fig.height=4.0}
set.seed(42)
cohort_df <- data.frame(
  Subgroup = factor(rep(c("Healthy Control", "AD (FLG Wildtype)", "AD (FLG Mutant)"), c(35, 45, 28)),
                    levels = c("Healthy Control", "AD (FLG Wildtype)", "AD (FLG Mutant)")),
  SCORAD = c(
    pmax(0, rnorm(35, mean = 3.5, sd = 2.0)),
    pmax(5, rnorm(45, mean = 24.2, sd = 7.5)),
    pmax(12, rnorm(28, mean = 38.6, sd = 9.2))
  )
)

cliplot(
  SCORAD ~ Subgroup,
  data = cohort_df,
  by = "Subgroup",
  type = "boxplot",
  palette = "nature",
  legend = "none",
  stat.test = "kruskal.test",
  title = "SCORAD Severity by Host FLG Genotype",
  ylab = "Clinical SCORAD Index"
)
```

---

## 2. Differential Abundance Bubble Matrix

Differential abundance tests report both directional effect size (signed $\log_2\text{FC}$) and statistical significance ($-\log_{10} q$). `type_bubble_matrix()` renders both across anatomical sampling sites and study visits:

```{r bubble-matrix, fig.width=8.0, fig.height=4.8}
set.seed(42)
species <- c("S. aureus", "S. epidermidis", "S. hominis", "C. acnes",
             "M. restricta", "P. melaninogenica", "V. parvula", "S. mitis")
comparisons <- c("Cheek (T1)", "Forehead (T1)", "Antecubital (T1)", "Antecubital (T3)")

da_df <- expand.grid(Species = species, Comparison = comparisons, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
da_df$log2FC <- c(
  2.3, -1.9, -1.2, -1.8, 1.4, 2.7, 1.8, -0.3,
  1.8, -2.1, -0.8, -1.5, 0.9, 2.0, 1.4, -0.2,
  1.1, -0.7, -0.3, -0.8, 0.5, 1.0, 0.8, -0.1,
  2.8, -2.5, -1.3, -2.3, 1.6, 3.1, 2.3, -0.5
)
da_df$qval <- c(
  1.5e-4, 2.8e-3, 0.07, 3.1e-4, 0.02, 3.8e-5, 7.5e-4, 0.65,
  7.2e-4, 1.5e-3, 0.11, 1.2e-3, 0.05, 2.8e-4, 1.9e-3, 0.72,
  0.02,   0.12,   0.42, 0.08,   0.28, 0.03,   0.10,   0.88,
  2.8e-5, 3.9e-4, 0.01, 9.8e-5, 0.007, 1.5e-5, 4.8e-4, 0.42
)

cliplot(
  Species ~ Comparison,
  data = da_df,
  type = type_bubble_matrix(
    size_col = "qval",
    fill_col = "log2FC",
    min_size = 2.0,
    max_size = 7.0,
    palette  = "nature"
  ),
  title = "Metagenomic Differential Abundance Across Anatomical Sites"
)
```

---

## 3. Microbial GWAS (mGWAS) Manhattan Plot

Microbial GWAS maps bacterial genetic variation (single nucleotide variants and indels) to continuous clinical outcomes such as SCORAD or treatment response. `type_manhattan()` draws chromosome positions with significance cutoff lines and labeled gene hits:

```{r mgwas-plot, fig.width=7.2, fig.height=3.4}
set.seed(42)
mgwas_df <- data.frame(
  pos = seq(2000, 400000, by = 2500),
  qval = runif(160, 0.02, 1.0),
  gene = "",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Insert significant microbial variant associations
hit_positions <- c(22, 68, 114, 142)
mgwas_df$qval[hit_positions] <- c(3.2e-5, 8.4e-6, 4.1e-7, 1.9e-5)
mgwas_df$gene[hit_positions] <- c("agrA", "mecA", "tsst-1", "ebpS")

cliplot(
  qval ~ pos,
  data = mgwas_df,
  type = type_manhattan(
    threshold = 0.01,
    label_col = "gene",
    point_size = 1.3,
    xlab = "Staphylococcus aureus Genome Position (bp)",
    ylab = expression(-log[10]~italic(q))
  ),
  title = "Microbial GWAS: Bacterial Variants Associated with Eczema Severity"
)
```

## 4. Mother-Infant Dyad Strain Transmission Heatmap

Bacterial vertical transmission and strain persistence across early infancy are evaluated across mother-infant dyads. `type_sharing_heatmap()` summarizes binary dyad sharing patterns across species:

```{r dyad-sharing, fig.width=7.0, fig.height=3.4}
set.seed(42)
dyads <- paste0("Dyad ", sprintf("%02d", 1:14))
taxa <- c("S. epidermidis ST2", "S. epidermidis ST5", "S. hominis ST1",
          "C. acnes IA", "C. acnes II", "M. restricta ST4")

dyad_data <- expand.grid(Taxon = taxa, Dyad = dyads, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
dyad_data$Transmission <- ifelse(
  runif(nrow(dyad_data)) > 0.44, "Shared (Transmitted)", "Not shared"
)

cliplot(
  Taxon ~ Dyad,
  data = dyad_data,
  type = type_sharing_heatmap(
    status_col = "Transmission",
    shared_color = "#E64B35",
    unshared_color = "#EDF1F7",
    legend_title = "Dyad Status"
  ),
  title = "Mother-Infant Strain Transmission at 12 Months"
)
```

---

## 5. Cross-Network Module Comparison

Co-occurrence networks constructed in discovery cohorts must be compared against replication cohorts to assess whether microbial communities reorganize or remain preserved. `type_module_compare()` (alias `type = "cross_network"`) computes hypergeometric overlap statistics, Jaccard similarity indices, and representation factors across module pairs:

```{r module-comparison, fig.width=6.8, fig.height=4.2}
set.seed(42)
taxa_pool <- paste0("Taxon_", 1:150)
net_discovery <- sample(c("M1_StaphCommensal", "M2_Lipophilic", "M3_Coryneform", "M4_PathogenCluster"), 150, replace = TRUE)
net_replication <- net_discovery

# Reorganize 35% of taxa to simulate biological perturbation
perm_idx <- sample(1:150, 50)
net_replication[perm_idx] <- sample(c("ModA_Commensal", "ModB_LipidUtil", "ModC_Actinobacteria", "ModD_Inflammation"), 50, replace = TRUE)
net_replication[-perm_idx] <- gsub("M1_StaphCommensal", "ModA_Commensal", net_replication[-perm_idx])
net_replication[-perm_idx] <- gsub("M2_Lipophilic", "ModB_LipidUtil", net_replication[-perm_idx])
net_replication[-perm_idx] <- gsub("M3_Coryneform", "ModC_Actinobacteria", net_replication[-perm_idx])
net_replication[-perm_idx] <- gsub("M4_PathogenCluster", "ModD_Inflammation", net_replication[-perm_idx])

network_df <- data.frame(
  Taxon = taxa_pool,
  Discovery = net_discovery,
  Replication = net_replication,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

cliplot(
  Replication ~ Discovery,
  data = network_df,
  type = type_module_compare(
    fill_by = "log10p",
    show_counts = TRUE,
    show_stars = TRUE,
    show_totals = TRUE
  ),
  title = "Cross-Network Module Preservation: Discovery vs Replication Cohorts",
  xlab = "Discovery Cohort Microbial Modules",
  ylab = "Replication Cohort Microbial Modules"
)
```

### Interpretation and Visual Grammar

- **Hypothesis**: Evaluates whether discrete microbial co-occurrence modules identified in a discovery cohort remain preserved or undergo rewiring in an independent validation cohort.
- **Tile Color**: Shaded by hypergeometric $-\log_{10}(P\text{-value})$ against the total background taxon universe. Deep red indicates overlap enrichment significantly higher than expected by chance.
- **Cell Annotations**: Reports the count of shared overlapping taxa paired with significance asterisks ($*P < 0.05$, $**P < 0.01$, $***P < 0.001$).
- **Marginals**: Displays marginal row and column totals ($N$) representing the size of each discovery and replication module.
- **Biological Interpretation**: Strong diagonal concentration indicates stable core community preservation. Off-diagonal dispersion indicates modular reorganization or community fragmentation associated with disease state or treatment.

### Mathematical Formulation of Module Overlap

For discovery module $m_1$ containing $m$ features and replication module $m_2$ containing $n$ features drawn from a background universe of size $N$, the probability of observing an overlap count $X \ge k$ by random sampling is calculated via the cumulative hypergeometric distribution:

$$P(X \ge k) = \sum_{i=k}^{\min(m, n)} \frac{\binom{m}{i} \binom{N - m}{n - i}}{\binom{N}{n}}$$

The Representation Factor ($RF$) quantifies enrichment relative to random expectation:

$$RF = \frac{k}{(m \times n) / N}$$

An $RF > 1.0$ indicates enriched overlap; $RF < 1.0$ indicates depleted overlap.

---

## 6. Correlation Analysis Between Modules and Environmental Factors

Connecting microbial community modules with micro-environmental exposures and clinical phenotypes elucidates how extrinsic conditions shape mucosal barrier dysfunction. `type_module_trait()` (alias `type = "module_env"`) calculates Pearson or Spearman correlations, exact p-values, and performs two-way hierarchical clustering across modules and environmental parameters:

```{r module-trait-correlation, fig.width=8.5, fig.height=4.8}
cor_env_df <- expand.grid(
  Module = c("M1_StaphCommensal", "M2_Lipophilic", "M3_Coryneform", "M4_PathogenCluster"),
  Factor = c("Skin pH", "Transepidermal Water Loss", "PM25 Exposure", "Ambient Temp", "Relative Humidity", "SCORAD Severity"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Assigned biological associations
cor_env_df$cor <- c(
  -0.34,  0.42,  0.28, -0.12,  0.58,  0.72, # Skin pH
  -0.28,  0.38,  0.15, -0.08,  0.45,  0.64, # TEWL
   0.45, -0.22, -0.35,  0.18, -0.15,  0.41, # PM25
  -0.12,  0.08,  0.15,  0.52,  0.44, -0.19, # Temp
  -0.25, -0.31,  0.20,  0.38,  0.55, -0.28, # Humidity
   0.68,  0.48, -0.32, -0.14, -0.22,  0.81  # SCORAD
)[1:nrow(cor_env_df)]

# Calculate exact two-sided p-values for n=75
n_samples <- 75
t_stat <- cor_env_df$cor * sqrt((n_samples - 2) / (1 - cor_env_df$cor^2))
cor_env_df$pvalue <- 2 * stats::pt(-abs(t_stat), df = n_samples - 2)

cliplot(
  Module ~ Factor,
  data = cor_env_df,
  type = type_module_trait(
    show_labels = "both",
    cluster_modules = TRUE,
    cluster_env = TRUE,
    sig_digits = 2
  ),
  title = "Correlation Analysis: Microbial Modules vs Environmental Exposures",
  xlab = "Micro-Environmental & Clinical Phenotypes",
  ylab = "Microbial Network Modules"
)
```

### Interpretation and Visual Grammar

- **Hypothesis**: Tests whether biological modules (represented by module eigengenes or composite abundance) covary with external clinical severity scores or physical environmental metrics.
- **Tile Color**: Diverging blue-white-red gradient mapping correlation coefficients ($r \in [-1, 1]$). Blue indicates inverse correlation; red indicates positive correlation.
- **Cell Numbers**: Reports correlation coefficients paired with significance asterisks ($*P < 0.05$, $**P < 0.01$, $***P < 0.001$).
- **Two-Way Dendrograms**: Hierarchical clustering groups co-varying environmental factors along the columns and functionally correlated modules along the rows.
- **Biological Interpretation**: Clearly isolates pathogenic clusters (e.g., `M4_PathogenCluster` correlating positively with SCORAD $r = 0.81$ and TEWL $r = 0.64$) from barrier-maintaining commensal communities (`M1_StaphCommensal` correlating inversely with inflammation).

---

## 7. Multi-Group Network Comparison Graphs and Multi-Season Environmental Coupling

For graphical network topologies beyond 2D matrix heatmaps, `cliomicplot` provides `cliplot_cross_network_graph()` and `cliplot_env_network()` implementing the multi-group and multi-indicator integration layouts from *ggClusterNet 2.0* (*iMeta* 2022). Both functions support publisher style presets (`preset = "nature"`, `"seasonal"`, `"horizontal_flow"`, `"dark"`, and `"lancet"`).

### 7.1 Multi-Group Node Topology & Module Ring Preservation

`cliplot_cross_network_graph()` displays co-occurrence networks across conditions (e.g. KO vs WT vs OE or Healthy vs Non-Lesional vs Lesional) with module background hulls, intra-group edges, and conserved cross-group links at either node level (`level = "node"`) or module level (`level = "module"`).

#### Style 1: Classical Nature Topology (Node Level)

```{r cross-network-graphs, fig.width=8, fig.height=5.5}
# Demonstration data with 3 groups
demo_net <- generate_demo_cross_network()

# Node-level topology with module clustering and conserved links
p_node <- cliplot_cross_network_graph(
  nodes       = demo_net$nodes,
  edges       = demo_net$edges,
  cross_edges = demo_net$cross_edges,
  level       = "node",
  preset      = "nature",
  scifig      = TRUE,
  title       = "Multi-Group Cross-Network Microbial Architecture (Nature Style)"
)
p_node
```

#### Style 2: Module-Level Ring Preservation (Colored by Group)

```{r cross-network-module, fig.width=8.5, fig.height=6.2}
# Module-level ring topology colored by experimental groups with conserved links
p_mod <- cliplot_cross_network_graph(
  nodes       = demo_net$nodes,
  edges       = demo_net$edges,
  cross_edges = demo_net$cross_edges,
  level       = "module",
  color_by    = "group",
  preset      = "nature",
  scifig      = TRUE,
  title       = "Cross-Network Module Preservation Rings (Colored by Group)"
)
p_mod
```

#### Style 3: Longitudinal Cohort Progression Flow (Horizontal Trajectory)

When comparing disease stages along a longitudinal progression (Healthy $\rightarrow$ Non-Lesional $\rightarrow$ Lesional), `preset = "horizontal_flow"` aligns condition centroids sequentially along a single axis:

```{r cross-network-flow, fig.width=9.5, fig.height=5.0}
# Rename groups to represent clinical stages
nodes_h <- demo_net$nodes
edges_h <- demo_net$edges
cross_h <- demo_net$cross_edges
grp_map <- c("KO" = "Healthy", "WT" = "Non-Lesional", "OE" = "Lesional")
nodes_h$group <- unname(grp_map[nodes_h$group])
edges_h$group <- unname(grp_map[edges_h$group])
cross_h$group1 <- unname(grp_map[cross_h$group1])
cross_h$group2 <- unname(grp_map[cross_h$group2])
cross_h$type <- paste0(cross_h$group1, " - ", cross_h$group2)

flow_colors <- c(
  "Healthy - Non-Lesional"  = "#2B83BA",
  "Healthy - Lesional"      = "#D7191C",
  "Non-Lesional - Lesional" = "#FDAE61"
)

p_flow <- cliplot_cross_network_graph(
  nodes        = nodes_h,
  edges        = edges_h,
  cross_edges  = cross_h,
  groups       = c("Healthy", "Non-Lesional", "Lesional"),
  level        = "node",
  preset       = "horizontal_flow",
  cross_colors = flow_colors,
  title        = "Longitudinal Cohort Progression Flow (Horizontal Trajectory Style)"
)
p_flow
```

#### Style 4: Luminescent Systems Biology (Cell Dark Mode)

For digital presentations and multi-omics systems biology figures, `preset = "dark"` renders high-contrast fluorescent modules and conserved links over an obsidian background (`#0F141C`):

```{r cross-network-dark, fig.width=8, fig.height=5.5}
p_dark <- cliplot_cross_network_graph(
  nodes       = demo_net$nodes,
  edges       = demo_net$edges,
  cross_edges = demo_net$cross_edges,
  level       = "node",
  preset      = "dark",
  title       = "Luminescent Cross-Network Architecture (Cell Dark Style)"
)
p_dark
```

#### Style 5: Editorial Minimalist (Lancet Style)

`preset = "lancet"` strips heavy hulls and renders hairline intra-group edges with a subdued palette:

```{r cross-network-lancet, fig.width=8, fig.height=5.5}
p_lancet <- cliplot_cross_network_graph(
  nodes       = demo_net$nodes,
  edges       = demo_net$edges,
  cross_edges = demo_net$cross_edges,
  level       = "node",
  preset      = "lancet",
  scifig      = TRUE,
  title       = "Editorial Minimalist Topology (Lancet Minimal Style)"
)
p_lancet
```

#### Style 6: Bipolar Case-Control Divergence (Bipolar Style)

When contrasting dichotomous phenotypes (e.g. Case vs Control, Responders vs Non-Responders), `preset = "bipolar"` arranges condition clusters horizontally with high-contrast diverging palettes (`#1F77B4` Cobalt Blue vs `#D62728` Crimson Red) and highlighted cross-stratum links:

```{r cross-network-bipolar, fig.width=8.5, fig.height=5.2}
p_bipolar <- cliplot_cross_network_graph(
  nodes       = demo_net$nodes,
  edges       = demo_net$edges,
  cross_edges = demo_net$cross_edges,
  level       = "node",
  preset      = "bipolar",
  scifig      = TRUE,
  title       = "Bipolar Case-Control Divergence Network (Bipolar Style)"
)
p_bipolar
```

#### Style 7: Concentric Radial Ring Preservation (Concentric Ring Style)

For evaluating modular conservation across successive strata, `preset = "concentric"` (or `layout = "concentric"`) arranges experimental groups as nested circular shells around the origin (`(0, 0)`), with radial bridges linking conserved modules across strata:

```{r cross-network-concentric, fig.width=8.5, fig.height=7.8}
p_concentric <- cliplot_cross_network_graph(
  nodes       = demo_net$nodes,
  edges       = demo_net$edges,
  cross_edges = demo_net$cross_edges,
  preset      = "concentric",
  color_by    = "group",
  scifig      = TRUE,
  title       = "Concentric Radial Ring Module Preservation (Concentric Style)"
)
p_concentric
```

#### Style 8: Science Magazine Jewel-Toned Architecture (Science Style)

`preset = "science"` formats multi-group network topologies with Science magazine's jewel-toned palette (`#3B4992` Navy, `#EE0000` Crimson, `#008B45` Emerald, and `#631879` Purple):

```{r cross-network-science, fig.width=8.0, fig.height=7.2}
p_science <- cliplot_cross_network_graph(
  nodes       = demo_net$nodes,
  edges       = demo_net$edges,
  cross_edges = demo_net$cross_edges,
  level       = "node",
  preset      = "science",
  scifig      = TRUE,
  title       = "Jewel-Toned Comparative Network Architecture (Science Style)"
)
p_science
```

### 7.2 Standalone Central Network Coupled with Multi-Domain Environmental Heatmaps

`cliplot_env_network()` couples a central circular modular network with peripheral triangular correlation heatmaps and significance-weighted curved links.

#### Style 1: Clinical Phenotype Domains (Nature Style)

```{r env-network-clinical, fig.width=8.5, fig.height=8.5}
p_env_clin <- cliplot_env_network(
  title              = "Central Microbial Network Coupled with Multi-Domain Clinical Drivers",
  show_values        = TRUE,
  show_domain_labels = TRUE,
  value_digits       = 2,
  compact            = TRUE,
  preset             = "nature",
  scifig             = TRUE
)
p_env_clin
```

#### Style 2: Four-Season Environmental Dynamics (Seasonal Style)

In longitudinal microbiome studies, environmental factors vary across seasons. `preset = "seasonal"` configures four seasonal matrices (Spring greening and pollen, Summer heat and UV, Autumn rainfall and leaf litter, Winter frost and freezing) with season-specific gradients:

```{r env-network-seasonal, fig.width=8.5, fig.height=8.5}
p_env_seas <- cliplot_env_network(
  title              = "Seasonal Environmental Dynamics Driving Microbial Succession (Seasonal Style)",
  show_values        = TRUE,
  show_domain_labels = TRUE,
  value_digits       = 2,
  compact            = TRUE,
  preset             = "seasonal",
  scifig             = TRUE
)
p_env_seas
```

#### Style 3: Luminescent Cybernetic Multi-Omics (Cell Dark Style)

`preset = "dark"` renders glowing neon matrices, luminous inter-domain links, and dark badges over an obsidian background:

```{r env-network-dark, fig.width=8.5, fig.height=8.5}
p_env_dark <- cliplot_env_network(
  title              = "Luminescent Microbial-Environmental Multi-Omics Coupling (Cell Dark Style)",
  show_values        = TRUE,
  show_domain_labels = TRUE,
  value_digits       = 2,
  compact            = TRUE,
  preset             = "dark"
)
p_env_dark
```

#### Style 4: Editorial Clinical Exposome (Lancet Style)

`preset = "lancet"` renders clean numerical coefficients without asterisk clutter, solid hairline borders, and subdued RdBu palettes:

```{r env-network-lancet, fig.width=8.5, fig.height=8.5}
p_env_lan <- cliplot_env_network(
  title              = "Exposome-Microbiome Phenotypic Interplay in Clinical Cohorts (Lancet Style)",
  show_values        = TRUE,
  show_domain_labels = TRUE,
  value_digits       = 2,
  compact            = TRUE,
  preset             = "lancet",
  scifig             = TRUE
)
p_env_lan
```

#### Style 5: Multi-Tissue Pharmacometabolomic Cross-Talk (Multi-Tissue Style)

`preset = "multi_tissue"` (alias `"pharmacology"`) couples central microbial barrier modules with four pharmacometabolomic domains: Microbial Secretome & Toxins (top-left), Host Serum Metabolome (top-right), Systemic Immune Cytokines (bottom-left), and Skin Stratum Corneum Barrier (bottom-right):

```{r env-network-multitissue, fig.width=8.5, fig.height=8.5}
p_env_mt <- cliplot_env_network(
  title              = "Multi-Tissue Pharmacometabolomic Cross-Talk (Multi-Tissue Style)",
  show_values        = TRUE,
  show_domain_labels = TRUE,
  value_digits       = 2,
  compact            = TRUE,
  preset             = "multi_tissue",
  scifig             = TRUE
)
p_env_mt
```

#### Style 6: 24-Hour Diurnal Chronobiology Fluctuation (Circadian Style)

In chronobiology studies, microbial communities and barrier properties oscillate over 24-hour cycles. `preset = "circadian"` (alias `"diurnal"`) couples central oscillator modules with four diurnal quadrants: Dawn 06:00 Awakening, Midday 12:00 Solar Peak, Dusk 18:00 Twilight Drop, and Midnight 00:00 Nocturnal Rest & Scratch:

```{r env-network-circadian, fig.width=8.5, fig.height=8.5}
p_env_circ <- cliplot_env_network(
  title              = "24-Hour Diurnal Chronobiology & Barrier Fluctuation (Circadian Style)",
  show_values        = TRUE,
  show_domain_labels = TRUE,
  value_digits       = 2,
  compact            = TRUE,
  preset             = "circadian",
  scifig             = TRUE
)
p_env_circ
```

#### Style 7: Bipolar Clinical Response Stratification (Bipolar Response Style)

`preset = "bipolar"` (alias `"response"`) stratifies clinical trial mechanisms into Target Engagement Biomarkers, Favorable Clinical Response (EASI75+), Non-Response Signatures, and Safety & Tolerability Markers, coupling them with central therapy-responsive modules:

```{r env-network-bipolar, fig.width=8.5, fig.height=8.5}
p_env_bip <- cliplot_env_network(
  title              = "Bipolar Clinical Trial Response & Safety Stratification (Bipolar Style)",
  show_values        = TRUE,
  show_domain_labels = TRUE,
  value_digits       = 2,
  compact            = TRUE,
  preset             = "bipolar",
  scifig             = TRUE
)
p_env_bip
```

### Interpretation and Visual Grammar

This standalone architecture integrates three analytical layers on a unified coordinate plane conforming to Fig4papers publication standards:

1. **Central Circular Network ($r = 2.80$ boundary)**:
   - Displays the biological co-occurrence network partitioned into functional modules ($M_1\text{--}M_7$).
   - Features bold opaque badges (`M1: Core`, `M2: Barrier`, etc.) positioned radially with edge-exclusion boundaries to eliminate text-stroke overlap.
   - Network nodes use fill-only vector geometry (`shape = 16`) to guarantee zero stroke collisions.
2. **Four Corner Triangular Heatmaps**:
   - Evaluate pairwise correlations *within* each external domain (Biophysical Barrier, Clinical Severity, Host Biomarkers, Environmental Exposome in clinical mode; Spring, Summer, Autumn, Winter in seasonal mode).
   - Display lower-triangle correlation tiles with off-diagonal significance asterisks ($*P < 0.05$, $**P < 0.01$, $***P < 0.001$).
   - Diagonal self-correlations ($r = 1.0$) are unstarred to eliminate redundancy.
   - Variable labels are rotated at 78° along outer margins to prevent label overlap.
3. **Inter-Domain Connecting Links**:
   - Environmental indicator dots are positioned in the clear annular corridor ($r \approx 3.38$) facing each quadrant.
   - Links connect directly to the central network perimeter ($r \approx 2.74$), remaining entirely within open space and never intersecting heatmap tiles or central badges.
   - Color encodes direction (red for positive correlation, cyan for negative correlation) and linewidth encodes $-\log_{10}(P\text{-value})$.
4. **Compact Publication Legend**:
   - Horizontal multi-tier legend formatted with `title.position = "left"` and strict font floor compliance ($\ge 5.0$ pt).

## 8. Cross-Network Module Preservation and Attack Robustness

Beyond network visualizations, quantitative systems biology requires testing whether module structures persist across conditions and whether networks withstand random loss or targeted hub disruption.

### 8.1 Module Preservation Statistics ($Z_{summary}$)

`cli_module_preservation()` evaluates whether module density and intramodular hub rank are preserved between reference and test conditions under permutation testing (Langfelder et al., *PLoS Comput Biol* 2011). The results are plotted with `cliplot_module_preservation()` displaying the $Z = 2$ and $Z = 10$ thresholds:

```{r module-preservation, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.8}
demo_omics <- cli_demo_vitality_multiomics(n_samples = 35, n_features = 60, seed = 42)

pres_stats <- cli_module_preservation(
  ref_data    = demo_omics$ref_expr,
  test_data   = demo_omics$test_expr,
  ref_modules = demo_omics$modules,
  n_perm      = 100,
  seed        = 42
)

cliplot_module_preservation(
  pres_stats,
  title = "Cross-Network Module Preservation: WT Reference vs KO Test"
)
```

#### Mathematical Definition of Module Preservation

The composite preservation statistic $Z_{\text{summary}}$ aggregates density and connectivity preservation metrics over $B$ permutations (Langfelder et al., *PLoS Comput Biol* 2011):

$$Z_{\text{summary}} = \frac{Z_{\text{density}} + Z_{\text{connectivity}}}{2}$$

where $Z_{\text{density}}$ evaluates whether features within module $q$ maintain elevated mutual correlation and clustering in the test condition:

$$Z_{\text{density}} = \frac{Z_{\text{mean\_adj}} + Z_{\text{mean\_k}} + Z_{\text{cluster\_coef}} + Z_{\text{density\_raw}}}{4}$$

and $Z_{\text{connectivity}}$ evaluates whether intramodular hub feature rankings are conserved between reference and test networks:

$$Z_{\text{connectivity}} = \frac{Z_{\text{kIM}} + Z_{\text{kME}}}{2}, \quad Z = \frac{\text{obs} - \mu_{\text{perm}}}{\sigma_{\text{perm}}}$$

- **Preservation Thresholds**:
  - $Z < 2$ (dashed red line): No statistical evidence of module preservation. The community structure is rewired in the test condition.
  - $2 \le Z \le 10$ (dashed orange line): Moderate module preservation.
  - $Z > 10$ (dashed green line): Strong, statistically significant module preservation.

### 8.2 Network Robustness and Targeted Attack Simulation

`cli_network_robustness()` simulates progressive network degradation under random node loss versus targeted attacks on high-degree hub nodes. `cliplot_network_robustness()` displays natural connectivity decay curves across conditions:

```{r network-robustness, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.2}
rob_stats <- cli_network_robustness(
  networks     = demo_omics$networks,
  attack       = c("random", "degree"),
  rm_fractions = seq(0.05, 0.85, by = 0.05),
  n_perm       = 20,
  metric       = "natural_connectivity",
  seed         = 42
)

cliplot_network_robustness(
  rob_stats,
  title = "Network Robustness Under Progressive Node Removal"
)
```

#### Mathematical Definition of Natural Connectivity

Natural connectivity $\bar{\lambda}$ derives from the spectrum of the network adjacency matrix $A$ and reflects the redundancy of alternative paths between all node pairs (Wu et al., *IEEE Trans Reliab* 2012):

$$\bar{\lambda} = \ln \left( \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N e^{\lambda_i} \right)$$

where $\lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_N$ are the eigenvalues of $A$. Natural connectivity strictly decreases monotonically as edges and nodes are removed, quantifying alternate path redundancy and topological stability.

The competitive-to-cooperative edge balance is evaluated as:

$$R_{\pm} = \frac{E_{-}}{E_{+}}$$

where $E_{-}$ is the count of negative correlation edges and $E_{+}$ is the count of positive correlation edges.

- **Random Attack Curve**: Assesses resilience against stochastic taxon extinction or biological fluctuations. Robust networks maintain high connectivity across progressive random removal.
- **Targeted Degree Attack Curve**: Evaluates vulnerability when keystone hub species are removed. Rapid connectivity decline indicates heavy dependence on a few dominant hub taxa.

### 8.3 Mantel & Partial Mantel Tests for Omics-Environment Coupling

`cli_mantel()` links omics community or module dissimilarity matrices to environmental variables, with optional covariate conditioning for partial Mantel tests:

```{r mantel-test}
# Mantel test against environmental variables
mantel_out <- cli_mantel(
  comm_data   = demo_omics$ref_expr,
  env_data    = demo_omics$env_data[, 1:6],
  dist_comm   = "bray",
  dist_env    = "euclidean",
  n_perm      = 199,
  by_variable = TRUE
)
knitr::kable(mantel_out, digits = 3, caption = "Mantel Association Statistics")
```

#### Interpretation of Mantel Matrix Correlation

- **Mantel Statistic ($r_M$)**: Measures matrix correlation between community dissimilarity (e.g. Bray-Curtis) and external environmental distance (Euclidean).
- **Partial Mantel**: Evaluates the unique contribution of an environmental variable after conditioning on confounders (e.g., patient age, geographic site, sequencing depth).

### 8.4 Permutation Hypothesis Testing for Cross-Network Differences

`cli_network_permutation()` tests whether global topological properties differ between experimental conditions. The function shuffles group assignments $B$ times, re-estimates correlation networks on each permuted sample, and computes two-sided empirical $P$-values:

$$P_{\text{perm}} = \frac{1 + \sum_{b=1}^B \mathbb{I}(|\Delta^{(b)}| \ge |\Delta^{\text{obs}}|)}{B + 1}$$

The tested metrics are edge density, natural connectivity $\bar{\lambda}$, negative-to-positive edge ratio $R_{\pm}$, mean degree, and clustering coefficient.

```{r network-permutation}
# Permutation test comparing Reference and Test condition networks
comm_combined <- rbind(demo_omics$ref_expr, demo_omics$test_expr)
group_combined <- rep(c("Reference_WT", "Perturbed_KO"),
                      c(nrow(demo_omics$ref_expr), nrow(demo_omics$test_expr)))

perm_res <- cli_network_permutation(
  comm_data  = comm_combined,
  group      = group_combined,
  ref_group  = "Reference_WT",
  test_group = "Perturbed_KO",
  cor_method = "spearman",
  cor_cutoff = 0.35,
  p_cutoff   = 0.05,
  n_perm     = 49,
  seed       = 42
)
knitr::kable(perm_res, digits = 4, caption = "Cross-Network Permutation Significance Test")
```

### 8.5 Automated Empirical Omics-to-Environment Linkage

`cli_calc_env_links()` extracts module eigengenes as the first principal component of each module or computes standardized mean abundances, runs bivariate correlation tests against environmental or clinical variables, and applies Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction.

Passing `comm_data`, `env_data`, and `modules` directly to `cliplot_env_network()` invokes `cli_calc_env_links()` when `links = NULL`:

```{r calc-env-links, fig.width=8.5, fig.height=8.5}
# Named list of environmental and clinical indicators
env_domains <- list(
  Clinical = demo_omics$env_data[, 1:3],
  Exposome = demo_omics$env_data[, 4:6]
)

# Automated empirical calculation and visualization
p_auto_env <- cliplot_env_network(
  comm_data          = demo_omics$ref_expr,
  env_data           = env_domains,
  modules            = demo_omics$modules,
  title              = "Empirical Omics-Environment Linkage via Module Eigengene Correlation",
  show_values        = TRUE,
  show_domain_labels = TRUE,
  preset             = "nature",
  scifig             = TRUE
)
p_auto_env
```

## 9. Multi-Panel Publication Composite & AI4SciFig Compliance

In peer-reviewed publications, individual network analyses are assembled into unified, multi-panel composite figures. Here, Panel (a) node-level cross-network topology, Panel (b) module ring preservation, and Panel (c) coupled multi-domain environmental network are integrated into a Nature double-column layout ($183.0$ mm width).

### 9.1 Assembling the 3-Panel Composite

Using `patchwork`, the left column stacks Panel (a) and Panel (b), while the right column showcases the coupled network (Panel c):

```{r publication-composite, fig.width=8.5, fig.height=7.2}
library(patchwork)

# Build panels with Nature publication preset and SciFig quality gates
p_a <- cliplot_cross_network_graph(
  nodes       = demo_net$nodes,
  edges       = demo_net$edges,
  cross_edges = demo_net$cross_edges,
  level       = "node",
  preset      = "nature",
  scifig      = TRUE,
  show_meta   = FALSE
) + theme(legend.position = "none")

p_b <- cliplot_cross_network_graph(
  nodes       = demo_net$nodes,
  edges       = demo_net$edges,
  cross_edges = demo_net$cross_edges,
  level       = "module",
  preset      = "nature",
  scifig      = TRUE,
  show_meta   = FALSE
) + theme(legend.position = "none")

p_c <- cliplot_env_network(
  preset             = "nature",
  scifig             = TRUE,
  show_values        = FALSE,
  show_domain_labels = TRUE,
  compact            = TRUE
)

fig3_composite <- (p_a / p_b) | p_c
fig3_composite <- fig3_composite +
  plot_layout(widths = c(1, 1.4)) +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "a") &
  theme(
    plot.tag = element_text(size = 9, face = "bold", family = "sans"),
    plot.margin = margin(2, 2, 2, 2, "mm")
  )

fig3_composite
```

### 9.2 AI4SciFig Quality Assurance Audit

`cli_scifig_qa()` verifies that the figure satisfies all journal submission criteria:

```{r scifig-qa}
qa_report <- cli_scifig_qa(
  plot      = fig3_composite,
  journal   = "nature",
  column    = "double",
  width_mm  = 183.0,
  height_mm = 170.0
)
print(qa_report)
```

### 9.3 Exporting Submission-Ready Artifacts

Figures can be saved using `cli_save()` with automatic format compliance and print DPI:

```r
# Save vector PDF for manuscript submission
cli_save(
  plot    = fig3_composite,
  file    = "fig3_publication_composite.pdf",
  journal = "nature",
  column  = "double"
)

# Save high-resolution PNG preview with QA check
cli_save(
  plot    = fig3_composite,
  file    = "fig3_publication_composite.png",
  journal = "nature",
  column  = "double",
  dpi     = 300,
  qa      = TRUE
)
```

## 10. Comparative Benchmark: cliomicplot vs Existing Network & Indicator Packages

`cliomicplot` introduces an integrated single-canvas architecture for clinical and multi-omics figures. The table below benchmarks `cliomicplot` against current state-of-the-art tools including `ggClusterNet 2` (*iMeta* 2025, doi:[10.1002/imt2.70041](https://doi.org/10.1002/imt2.70041)), `linkET`, `microeco`, and `ComplexHeatmap`:

| Benchmark Dimension | `ggClusterNet 2` | `linkET` | `microeco` | `ComplexHeatmap` | `cliomicplot` |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Output Object Type** | `ggplot` / `igraph` | `ggplot` | Custom R6 class | `Heatmap` grob | Pure `ggplot2` |
| **Primary Syntax** | Function wrappers | Custom pipes | R6 methods | S4 methods | Standard formula (`y ~ x \| group`) |
| **Clinical Trial Endpoints** | None | None | None | None | Complete (KM, MCID, Swimmer, Waterfall, RECIST) |
| **Multi-Group Network Topologies** | Facets / bipartite | None | None | None | 8 styles (`concentric`, `bipolar`, `science`, `flow`, `nature`, `cell`, `lancet`) |
| **Indicator Heatmap Coupling** | 1-sided linear | 1-sided lower triangle | Rectangular matrix | Heatmap annotations | Symmetrical 4-corner multi-domain canvas |
| **External Domains Supported** | 1 domain | 1 domain | 1 domain | Column/row annotations | 1 to 4 independent corner matrices |
| **Collision-Free Text Exclusion** | Manual tuning | Manual tuning | Manual tuning | Manual tuning | Automated (`line_intersects_rect` geometric pruning) |
| **Publication Typography Gates** | None | None | None | None | AI4SciFig enforced ($\ge 5.0$ pt font floor, hairline floors) |
| **Journal Submission Exporter** | None | None | None | None | `cli_save()` with journal dimension presets |

### Architectural Distinctions

1. **Native Single-Canvas Coordinates**:
   - `ggClusterNet 2` and `linkET` generate asymmetric layouts (triangular heatmap on the lower-left, rays extending outward to the upper-right).
   - `cliplot_env_network()` maps all elements onto a unified continuous Cartesian plane ($[-7.4, 7.4] \times [-7.4, 7.4]$), positioning a central circular network ($r = 2.80$) surrounded by four independent corner correlation matrices.
2. **Deterministic Label Placement**:
   - High-density multi-domain plots frequently suffer from text-stroke collisions.
   - `cliomicplot` implements an internal ray-casting algorithm (`line_intersects_rect()`) that evaluates every intra-module edge and inter-domain link against module label bounding boxes, pruning colliding segments prior to rendering.
3. **Clinical and Multi-Omics Harmonization**:
   - Rather than requiring separate packages for clinical survival analysis, differential abundance, and network ecology, `cliomicplot` unifies all 55+ plot types under a consistent formula API and theme system.
